Believer's Baptism
bih-LEE-ver BAP-tiz-um
noun phrase / doctrine
Believer (from Old English gelyfan, to believe; one who places trust and confidence in a specific object or person) + baptism (Greek baptisma, from baptizō, to immerse, dip, or plunge). The phrase “believer's baptism” or credobaptism (from Latin credo, I believe) is the distinctive Baptist and Reformed Baptist teaching that water baptism in the name of the Trinity is properly administered only to those who make a credible confession of faith in Jesus Christ — not to infants or the unbaptized who have not yet confessed. The term emerged in polemical contrast to paedobaptism during the sixteenth-century Reformation debates.

See also: Believer's Baptism

Biblical Definition

Believer's baptism is the doctrine that water baptism is the New Testament's proper first act of obedience for one who has repented, believed, and confessed Jesus Christ as Lord — the enacted declaration of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, administered by immersion in water in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Acts pattern is consistently confess-then-baptize: Peter's Pentecost sermon ends with “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38); the Ethiopian eunuch confesses “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God” before Philip baptizes him (Acts 8:37–38). The theological ground is Romans 6:3–4: baptism enacts a death to the old life and a resurrection into the new, a transition that only a regenerate person can honestly confess to have undergone. Galatians 3:27 declares that “all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” — the clothing-language presupposes a prior reality (union with Christ through faith) that the baptism publicly enacts. The 1689 LBCF (29.2) is explicit: “None are to be baptized, but such as do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ.” Believer's baptism is thus not merely a different mode debate (immersion vs. sprinkling) but a different understanding of what the sign signifies and to whom it belongs: it belongs to the regenerate covenant community of the new covenant, whose members all know the Lord (Jer 31:34; Heb 8:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Believer's baptism (credobaptism) is the doctrine that water baptism is properly administered only to those who confess repentance and faith in Jesus Christ — as the enacted sign of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, following the consistent Acts pattern of confession-before-baptism.

BELIEVER'S BAPTISM. Also credobaptism (L. credo, I believe): the doctrine that Christian water baptism belongs properly and exclusively to those who make a credible confession of repentance and faith in Jesus Christ, because the sign represents a spiritual death and resurrection already accomplished by the Spirit through the regenerating Word.

2. The Acts pattern: (1) Peter's Pentecost sermon — repent, then be baptized (Acts 2:38); (2) Philip and the eunuch — if you believe with all your heart, you may be baptized (Acts 8:37); (3) Cornelius's household — received the Spirit first, then baptized (Acts 10:44–48); (4) Lydia — the Lord opened her heart, then her household was baptized (Acts 16:15). In every clear case the sequence is: God's saving work first, baptism as the responsive enacted confession second.

3. The new covenant logic (Jer 31:33–34; Heb 8:10–11): the new covenant, unlike the old, is characterized by universal inward knowledge of the Lord among all its members (“they shall all know me”). The covenant community is a regenerate community; its sign belongs to the regenerate.

4. The paedobaptist counter and the credobaptist response: paedobaptism applies the sign on the basis of covenant membership in a mixed community (as circumcision applied to Isaac before faith). Credobaptism holds that the new covenant has categorically different membership criteria — inward regeneration rather than physical descent — and therefore a categorically different sign protocol.

5. The 1689 LBCF position (29.1–2): believer's baptism by immersion is the New Testament pattern; it is not a mere mode preference but the theologically determined connection between the sign (immersion into water) and the thing signified (burial and resurrection with Christ).

Key Scripture

Acts 8:37 — "And Philip said, “If you believe with all your heart, you may.” And he answered and said, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”"

Acts 8:38 — "And he ordered the chariot to stop. And they both went down into the water — Philip as well as the eunuch — and he baptized him."

Acts 2:38 — "Peter said to them, “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."

Gal 3:27 — "For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ."

Modern Corruption

Believer's baptism has been corrupted by the paedobaptist tradition's application of the sign to the infants of covenant households, collapsing the new covenant's regenerate-only membership criterion into the old covenant's mixed-community pattern — and by the evangelical reduction of baptism to a meaningless social ceremony with no doctrinal weight.

expand to see more

The paedobaptist argument — that infant baptism is the new covenant equivalent of circumcision, administered on the basis of covenant household membership rather than personal confession — rests on an analogy between the old and new covenant communities that the New Testament does not sustain in the direction paedobaptism requires. Colossians 2:11–12 invokes the circumcision analogy for believer's baptism, not for infant baptism: the “circumcision made without hands” (spiritual regeneration) is the thing to which water baptism corresponds in the passage, and it is accomplished by the Spirit in the heart before the outward sign. The Baptist position is that the new covenant community is explicitly a community whose members “all know me” (Jer 31:34) — inward knowledge that cannot be attributed to an unbaptized infant but only to one the Spirit has regenerated.

The evangelical reduction of baptism to a public testimony — “just a symbol, take it or leave it” — is a different corruption: it evacuates the sign of its enacted gospel-content. The New Testament does not treat baptism as an optional addendum to conversion; it treats it as the first enacted obedience of the new believer, inseparably linked to repentance and faith (Acts 2:38), to union with Christ in death and resurrection (Rom 6:3–4), and to clothing oneself with Christ (Gal 3:27). A theology of baptism as mere public declaration misses the richness of the enacted gospel that Christ designed the sign to convey.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Believer's baptism roots in the new covenant's regenerate-community principle (Jer 31:33–34), in the Acts pattern of confession-before-baptism, in the Pauline theology of baptism as the enacted sign of union with Christ in His death and resurrection, and in the 1689 LBCF as the defining confessional anchor.

expand to see more

Jeremiah 31:33–34 — the new covenant's distinctive: “they shall all know me”; the covenant community is constituted by inward regenerating knowledge, not physical descent — the foundational principle that determines who receives its sign

Acts pattern — Acts 2:38; 8:37–38; 10:44–48; 16:31–33: the consistent apostolic order is believe-and-repent, then be baptized; no counterexample in Acts involves baptism administered to someone who has not first confessed faith

Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12 — baptism as enacted death and resurrection: the sign signifies a spiritual event (dying to the old life; rising in Christ's resurrection) that has already occurred in the regenerate person who receives it

Galatians 3:27 — clothing with Christ: baptism as the public enacted clothing of oneself with Christ, which presupposes that Christ is already possessed by faith; the sign clothes what faith already holds

1689 LBCF 29.1–2 — the confessional anchor: “None are to be baptized but such as do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ”; immersion as the mode fitted to the sign's burial-and-resurrection meaning

Usage

"The Philip-and-eunuch narrative (Acts 8:26–40) is the paradigmatic believer's baptism account: Scripture reading, gospel explanation, explicit confession of faith (“I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God”), immediate baptism, and the joy that follows. The sequence is not ceremony first and faith later; it is faith operative, then the enacted sign of that faith. The eunuch's joy (Acts 8:39) follows the baptism because the baptism followed and expressed the faith, not as a magical addition to it."

"Titus 3:5 — “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit” — uses water-language for regeneration, but the agency is the Spirit (not the water itself). This verse supports the believer's baptism framework: the spiritual washing (regeneration by the Spirit) is the real event; the water baptism is the outward enacted sign of what the Spirit has already accomplished in the regenerate heart."

"The paedobaptist-credobaptist debate is a genuine intramural Reformed disagreement, not a salvation issue. The Baptist position of the 1689 LBCF holds that the new covenant's explicitly regenerate membership criterion (Jer 31:34; Heb 8:11) demands a different sign protocol than the old covenant's mixed-community circumcision — and that the Acts pattern of believe-then-baptize is the apostolic settlement of the question."
